recent_posts.title: How Major Reasoning Models Converge to the Same “Brain” as They Model Reality Increasingly Better
recent_posts.summary: Research from MIT and other groups suggests that as AI models scale up, they independently converge toward the same internal representation of reality — regardless of whether they were trained on text, images, or audio. This 'Platonic Representation Hypothesis' proposes that sufficiently capable models stop memorizing tasks and instead build a statistical model of reality itself. Three forces drive this convergence: task generality (there's only one optimal world model), model capacity, and a simplicity bias in deep networks. The phenomenon parallels how human brains integrate multimodal inputs into a unified perception of the world, and has implications for robotics and AGI.

recent_posts.title: When the Uncertainty Is Bigger Than the Shock: Scenario Modelling for English Local Elections
recent_posts.summary: A data science case study applying scenario modelling to 2026 English local elections across 64 authorities. Six scenarios are tested against a historical baseline, revealing that even the strongest scenario shock (a +4pp challenger surge) represents only 13% of the median calibrated uncertainty band. The key insight: scenario shocks are smaller than historical forecast error, making rankings without uncertainty intervals misleading. The methodology uses backtest residuals as an empirical bootstrap distribution for uncertainty bands, mean-centered at the tier level. Two asymmetric scenarios illustrate design principles: isolate one mechanism per scenario for falsifiability (S4), and log guardrails even when they don't bind (S5). The model is frozen, hashed, and reproducible, with a public accuracy audit planned post-election.

recent_posts.title: Why LLMs should explain decisions not make them in weather agents
recent_posts.summary: A physicist-turned-ML-engineer argues against using LLMs to make threshold-based decisions in weather monitoring agents. Drawing on chaos theory and meteorological expertise, the author explains why probabilistic models shouldn't replace deterministic rules for well-defined decision boundaries. The post presents Skygent, an open-source weather change detection agent with a five-layer architecture where a Python evaluator handles all threshold logic and the LLM is invoked only to narrate already-made decisions. This hybrid approach enables 204 unit tests with zero LLM dependencies, reduces API calls from ~28 to 1-2 per week per event, and produces fully explainable, reproducible alerts. The core principle: use LLMs to explain decisions, not to replace well-defined ones.

recent_posts.title: Building a self-healing hallucination detection layer for RAG systems
recent_posts.summary: A developer building a RAG-powered assistant discovered that even when retrieval returns the correct document, the LLM can still generate contradictory answers. To address this, they built a lightweight self-healing layer in pure Python that detects and corrects hallucinations before they reach users. The system identifies five failure patterns: confident-but-ungrounded responses, factual contradictions, hallucinated entities, answer drift, and negation flips. Detection runs under 50ms using spaCy NER or a regex fallback with no external APIs or LLM judges. Three healing strategies fix bad answers in-place: contradiction patching (swapping wrong numbers/values), entity scrubbing (removing sentences with hallucinated names), and grounding rewrite (rebuilding the answer from top-ranked context sentences). A quality scoring system routes answers to ACCEPT, HEALED_ACCEPT, FALLBACK, or DISCARD tiers. An SQLite-backed drift monitor tracks answer consistency across process restarts. The system ships with 70 tests covering every named failure mode, including thread safety and persistence edge cases.

recent_posts.title: Single Agent vs Multi-Agent: When to Build a Multi-Agent System
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide to AI agent design covering core components (LLM, tools, memory), the ReAct reasoning loop, and when to choose single-agent vs multi-agent architectures. Includes a walkthrough of a Multi-Agent RAG Researcher project built with an orchestrator coordinating three worker agents (Retriever, Writer, Verifier), using Qdrant for vector search, Tavily for web search, SQLite for session memory, and a Gradio UI — with full setup instructions and GitHub repo.

recent_posts.title: How to Build an Efficient Knowledge Base for AI Models
recent_posts.summary: A practical 6-step guide to building a reliable knowledge base for AI models, covering data collection, cleaning and chunking, vectorization, storage in vector databases (Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate), retrieval optimization using hybrid search (BM25 + embeddings), and automated quality monitoring. Includes Python code for vector normalization, scalar/product quantization, hybrid search with RRF, and knowledge base health monitoring using DeepEval and TruLens. Also addresses common challenges like data quality errors, retrieval slowness, and scalability issues with concrete solutions such as HNSW indexing, horizontal sharding, and selective forgetting.

recent_posts.title: Playing Connect Four with Deep Q-Learning
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough of applying Deep Q-Learning (DQN) to the game of Connect Four, extending a prior tabular Sarsa framework. Key additions include a replay buffer for batched off-policy updates, a vectorized environment wrapper for parallel game simulation, and action masking for illegal moves. Results show the DQN clearly outperforms random play and learns offensive strategies, but plateaus around one million steps and struggles with defensive play. The post discusses the transition from on-policy to off-policy methods, Python parallelism limitations (GIL), and the need for specialization to push beyond general RL frameworks.

recent_posts.title: How AI Tools Generate Technical Debt in IoT Systems — and What to Do About It
recent_posts.summary: AI coding assistants accelerate IoT development but introduce four categories of technical debt: reproducing legacy patterns, generating quick fixes without architectural awareness, duplicating logic, and ignoring hardware constraints like memory limits and network bandwidth. In IoT/IIoT systems these issues are especially costly because bugs can propagate across thousands of physical devices simultaneously. Mitigation strategies include mandatory human code review, defining no-go zones for autonomous AI generation in critical firmware paths, regular refactoring cycles (at least every six months), and device-level monitoring beyond standard backend observability tools.

recent_posts.title: CSPNet explained with a from-scratch PyTorch implementation on DenseNet
recent_posts.summary: CSPNet (Cross Stage Partial Network) is a neural network design paradigm that reduces computational complexity of DenseNet while maintaining or improving accuracy. It works by splitting input feature maps into two parts channel-wise: one part skips the dense block entirely (reducing redundant gradient computation), while the other is processed normally. The two parts are then merged via transition layers. The post walks through the original paper's architecture variants (fusion first, fusion last, CSPDenseNet), experimental results showing 13-26% complexity reduction with accuracy improvements, and provides a complete from-scratch PyTorch implementation including Bottleneck, DenseBlock, FirstTransition, SecondTransition, and the full CSPDenseNet model with channel-splitting logic.

recent_posts.title: Inference Scaling (Test-Time Compute): Why Reasoning Models Raise Your Compute Bill
recent_posts.summary: Inference scaling (test-time compute) lets reasoning models like GPT o1 spend extra compute during generation to improve answer quality, but this dramatically increases token usage, latency, and costs. Hidden reasoning tokens never shown to users still incur billing charges. A Cost-Quality-Latency triangle framework helps teams decide when reasoning mode is worth it. Key insight: reasoning models can waste thousands of tokens on simple tasks like classification or formatting, where standard models perform equally well at a fraction of the cost. A task taxonomy (use/maybe/avoid) and selective routing policy can cut costs by up to 68% — over $740K/year in one example — by reserving reasoning tokens only for high-stakes, multi-step logic tasks. Governance practices like hard token caps, prompt complexity classifiers, and measuring cost-per-successful-task rather than cost-per-million-tokens are recommended for production deployments.
